summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing subscribers on DOCSIS cable modem termination systems using SNMP. It covers the controls an operator needs to manage the subscriber side of a cable data network.

eli5.summary: Cable internet companies need a way to check and control the equipment that serves many customers. This document defines the remote controls and gauges for it.

questions: snmp objects for cable modem termination systems
what is the docsis subscriber management mib
how does a cmts limit cpe ip addresses
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a cable operator control which hosts and which traffic sit behind each cable modem, enforced at the CMTS.

tldr.problem: Cable operators need to stop subscribers from spoofing addresses or running unauthorized services. Filtering in the cable modem alone can be defeated if a user tampers with the modem software.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB defines four tables on the CMTS that limit the IP addresses behind each modem and assign each modem to filter groups. The actual packet filtering reuses the Differentiated Services MIB of RFC 3289.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9141. Its compliance statements cover IPv4 only, because DOCSIS 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0 are not IPv6 capable.

today: RFC 4036 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9141. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4036 defines a part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing DOCSIS Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTS) with SNMP. Its goal is to protect the cable network from misuse by subscribers, such as address spoofing, service spoofing, or operation of unauthorized services.

The module resides at the CMTS, the first point in the public data network at which the cable operator controls physical access. It controls IP packet forwarding to and from each cable modem, and different modems may be accorded different treatment.

Much of it duplicates the DOCSIS Cable Device MIB (RFC 2669). The difference is where it runs: a malicious user might tamper with cable modem software and disable its filtering, but physical access to the CMTS is controlled by the operator, so this MIB is the more secure mechanism.
sections.eli5: The cable company does not want to trust the box in your house to follow the rules, so it puts the rule book on its own box that you cannot touch.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB has two capabilities: limiting the IP addresses behind a modem, and address and protocol filtering to and from a modem. It is built from four tables.

  • docsSubMgtCpeControlTable controls acceptance of subscriber host addresses behind a modem.
  • docsSubMgtCpeIpTable monitors the host addresses the CMTS believes exist behind the modem.
  • docsSubMgtCmFilterTable binds a modem to a set of filters.
  • docsSubMgtFilterGroupTable provides the object identifiers by which the Differentiated Services classifier selects a filter group.

The control and filter tables augment docsIfCmtsCmStatusTable from RFC 2670, and the address table extends it with an additional index, so each row is tied to a modem registered at the CMTS.

Because large numbers of modems share filtering characteristics, modems are grouped so they share common filter lists, rather than keeping a separate list per modem.
sections.eli5: There are four lists on the box: how many devices each customer may plug in, which devices the box has seen, which rule set each customer follows, and a menu of rule sets.

sections.title: Registration and Address Control
sections.content:
A modem gets its parameters over TFTP, passes many of them to the CMTS in the DOCSIS Registration message, and the values are digitally signed and verified by the CMTS. Filtering criteria are kept through SNMP at the CMTS, and registration only signals the index values for the rows that apply to that modem.

The CMTS creates rows in docsSubMgtCpeControlTable for each modem at registration. If the registration does not provide values, the CMTS applies the defaults: docsSubMgtCpeActiveDefault (false), docsSubMgtCpeMaxIpDefault (16) and docsSubMgtCpeLearnableDefault (true).

Rows in docsSubMgtCpeIpTable come from DOCSIS registration, from learning by the CMTS, or from an unspecified administrative mechanism. The CMTS may learn addresses by snooping source IP addresses; the learning mechanism is not defined. When subscriber management is active and a packet arrives from an unknown source address, it is added and forwarded if the table is below docsSubMgtCpeControlMaxCpeIp, and dropped if the table is at that limit. A limit of zero drops all CPE traffic from the modem.
sections.eli5: Each customer gets a limit on how many gadgets can use their connection. If a new gadget shows up and there is room, it is added to the list. If the list is full, it is turned away.

sections.title: Filter Groups and the Differentiated Services MIB
sections.content:
Filtering is built on the Classification, Counting and Drop facilities of the Differentiated Services MIB (RFC 3289). Implementations are expected to include several of its tables, such as the classifier, multi-field classifier, action, count action and algorithmic drop tables, with diffServAlgDropType set to alwaysDrop.

RFC 3289 assumes all packets in one direction on one interface are classified the same way. Filter groups extend this so different subscribers get different treatment. A filter group can be seen as a sub-interface, or as a field logically prepended to the packet before classification. That field has no existence outside the CMTS.

Classification runs twice. The first pass selects a filter group using the object identifiers from docsSubMgtFilterGroupTable. The second pass classifies on IP, TCP and UDP criteria, and its action may be a count and accept, a drop, or another RFC 3289 feature. Only the DOCSIS MAC cable interfaces are used for subscriber management.
sections.eli5: First the box looks at which customer group a packet belongs to. Then it checks the packet against that group's rule list and either counts it, lets it through, or throws it away.

sections.title: Modem Traffic and Subscriber Traffic
sections.content:
All traffic from or to a subscriber site is potentially suspect, even if it is sourced or sunk by the cable modem itself. So the MIB allows separate filter policies for the modem and for the hosts behind it. For example, modem policies may limit modems to server-subnet-only access while allowing a different scope to subscribers.

DOCSIS registration may signal four filter group indices: upstream and downstream, each for the modem and for the subscribers. The CMTS chooses solely by MAC address (source upstream, destination downstream). If it matches the modem, the modem pair is used, otherwise the subscriber pair. If the modem acts as a router instead of a bridging forwarder, only the modem pair is used.

If registration omits these values, all four are set to zero. Zero selects the default classification entry, so omission results in the default filtering, not in no filtering.
sections.eli5: The box checks whether a message is to or from the modem itself or a gadget behind it, and uses a different rule list for each.

sections.title: Tiny Fragment Attack Protection
sections.content:
Implementers are recommended to prevent the "tiny fragment" and "overlapping fragment" attacks on the TCP filtering tables, as discussed in RFC 1858 and RFC 3128. When filtering is enabled, the rules are:

  • Admit all packets with fragment offset of 2 or more.
  • Discard packets with fragment offset 1, or with fragment offset 0 and fragment payload length under 16.
  • Apply filtering rules to all packets with fragment offset 0.

The security section makes this binding: for TCP filtering to be effective, implementors MUST follow these recommendations.
sections.eli5: Sneaky senders can chop a message into tiny pieces to hide it from the guard. The rules throw out suspiciously tiny pieces so the guard sees enough to judge.

sections.title: Conformance and IPv4 Scope
sections.content:
The compliance statements require support only for IPv4 addresses, because DOCSIS 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0 are not IPv6 capable. IPv6 support is expected to need only new compliance statements in the module itself.

A conforming implementation is only required to support up to sixteen addresses per modem and thirty filter groups, and only nonvolatile storage for the Differentiated Services tables it uses. The module is registered as docsSubMgt at { mib-2 125 } in the SMI Numbers registry.
sections.eli5: The rules only promise to work for the older kind of internet addresses, and a box only has to handle a modest number of devices and rule groups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The limits can be compromised if the modem's identity or registration process is spoofed. The DOCSIS RFI and privacy specifications define mechanisms for assuring modem identity.

Unauthorized SETs could permit address spoofing and defeat of operator-defined packet filtering. Sensitive writable objects include the CPE control objects and the four docsSubMgtCmFilter objects. The most sensitive readable object is docsSubMgtCpeIpAddr, since the table reveals the current subscriber address pool.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Whoever can change the settings can switch off the guard, so only trusted people should get the keys, and the keys should be well protected.

items.text: Binds a modem to its filter groups.
